name: Crom Dubh

attributes.attribute: an Irish god or hero who appears as a pagan king in the legends of St. Patrick
site of the annual celebration named Crom Dubh, in Co. Mayo
sometimes the name of Patrick’s kingly adversary, possibly a humanized god
Domhnach Chrom Dubh, Crom Dubh's Sunday, is another name for the festival

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Crom Dubh is a legendary chieftain of pre-Christian Ireland. His name means black crescent in Irish. Oral tradition made him out of the old god Crom Crúaich. They gave the god human shape and a human story. Saint Patrick overcame him as the faith spread through the island. An older tale keeps the contest in a different key. Patrick had received three bulls. To Crom Dubh's mind he had been shy in thanks, saying only thanks to god as each beast arrived. Patrick set his words on three paper slips and weighed them against the bulls. The totals matched, and the chieftain converted at once. His defeat lives on in the calendar. Domhnach Chrom Dubh, his Sunday, is another name for Lughnasa, the Garland Sunday. It falls on the final Sunday of July or the first of August. That is the day of the Croagh Patrick climb. Many readers see in Patrick's royal adversary the elder god Crom Cruach wearing a human face.

okr.objective: Crom Dubh is a pagan king in St. Patrick’s legends who converts after a test with three bulls.
key_results: He appears as a pagan king who grew angry that Patrick gave only “thanks to god” for three bulls.
Patrick’s written thanks weighed the same as the bulls, and Crom Dubh converted.
His name titles the annual celebration at Croagh Patrick in Co. Mayo; the adversary is sometimes called Crom Cruach.
MacKillop glosses the name as black crescent and derives the chieftain from Crom Crúaich.
Patrick overcomes him in the stories of the island's evangelization.
His Sunday, Domhnach Chrom Dubh, names the Lughnasa or Garland Sunday of late July or early August.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore
